newsitem.title: USA: Dole falls further behind, Perot set to name VP.
newsitem.headline: Dole falls further behind, Perot set to name VP.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
Republican Bob Dole on Monday attacked President Bill Clinton's economic policies and questioned his intervention in Iraq, but the president retained a huge lead in two new polls.

As Clinton took the day off from the campaign trail to attend to affairs of state, a CNN/USA Today tracking poll gave the president a massive 21 percentage point advantage over Dole among likely voters, 55 percent to 34 percent. Texas billionaire Ross Perot trailed with 5 percent.
The daily poll began Sept. 4, when Clinton led by 17 points. Since then, he has gained and Dole has lost two percentage points.

A Harris poll of likely voters had Clinton leading by a more modest 15 points, 52 to 37 percent. Perot polled 7 percent. But Harris said Clinton's favourability rating was up to 59 percent, the best of his entire presidency.

In other campaign developments, Perot said he would name a running mate for his Reform Party ticket in a 30-minute advertising programme he has purchased on the CBS television network on Tuesday evening.

Responding to questions about his running mate, Perot said it would be "somebody who has the background, the experience and qualifications and more than anything else, the guts and integrity to deal with this."

Dole received more bad news from two new state polls. In Texas, which should be a safe Republican stronghold, Dole barely led Clinton, 44 percent to 41 percent. In Michigan, a key battleground state, Clinton led easily, 47 percent to 29 percent. Perot had a scant 4 percent in both polls.
Searching for a winning issue, Dole turned to foreign policy on Monday, issuing a statement questioning the outcome of Clinton's strategy in Iraq.

"The Clinton administration should be careful about making claims of success that events on the ground may not substantiate, and about giving assurances that it is unable or unwilling to fulfil, because the credibility of the United States is at stake," the statement said.

Campaigning in Georgia, Dole charged that Clinton's economic policies were raising interest rates and pricing Americans out of the housing market. At a home construction site in an Atlanta suburb, Dole said interest rates had risen one and a half percentage points since Clinton vetoed a Republican balanced budget plan last year.

He promised his ambitious proposal for a balanced budget and a 15 percent income tax cut would boost the economy and cut interest rates. "The government can help by lowering interest rates, lowering our federal spending, lowering the taxes and giving you an American opportunity, an opportunity to restore the American dream," he said.
Polls show Dole has made no headway to overcome deep public scepticism about his tax cutting proposal, which he launched in early August.

From Georgia, Dole travels to Tampa, Florida. Polls show Clinton, who spent two days campaigning there last week, has a shot at winning Florida in November, which would make him the first Democrat to carry the state in two decades.

Speaking to reporters on his plane, Dole said he was preparing for a series of debates with Clinton, tentatively scheduled to begin this month. He said representatives of his campaign would begin meeting with Clinton's camp on Thursday to work out details, adding that he had not started practising for the debates yet.
